messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Animator
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 70

# The Weight of the Waiting Room

Rajan is a fifty-year-old South Asian man who has worked as an animator for nearly two decades, spending his days building worlds frame by frame, controlling every detail of movement and expression. He is soft-spoken and precise, the kind of man who notices things others miss. He sits in sessions with his hands folded in his lap, and when he talks about his son, he looks just slightly to the left of wherever he is.

Four years ago, his son Arjun — then fourteen — collapsed during a cricket match in the backyard. By the time the ambulance arrived, Arjun had had a seizure. The diagnosis that followed was acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Rajan remembers the oncologist's exact words, the exact angle of light coming through the hospital blinds, the way his wife Priya gripped his forearm so hard she left marks. He remembers thinking that he needed to memorize everything, as though paying close enough attention might give him some control over what happened next.

For eighteen months, Arjun underwent chemotherapy. Rajan took a leave of absence from the studio and drove his son to treatments twice a week. He watched Arjun become someone smaller — thinner, quieter, exhausted in a way no teenager should be. There were two hospitalizations for infections, one of which landed Arjun in the ICU for five days. During those five days, Rajan did not sleep. He sat in a chair outside the unit and stared at the double doors, certain that if he looked away, something irreversible would happen. He has never entirely stopped believing that.

Arjun is now in remission. He is eighteen and applying to universities. By every medical measure, he is well. Rajan knows this. He also cannot fully feel it.

He returned to work two years ago, but the studio is a different place now. He sits at his desk and draws characters in motion — running, falling, catching themselves — and without warning, his chest tightens and the hospital comes back. Not as a memory he chooses to visit, but as something that arrives uninvited: the smell of antiseptic, the sound of an IV alarm, the specific quality of fluorescent light at three in the morning. He sets down his stylus and waits for it to pass. Sometimes it takes minutes. Sometimes the rest of the day is lost.

He does not sleep well. He wakes between two and four most mornings and lies still beside Priya, running through scenarios — what if the remission ends, what if there is a secondary cancer, what if he misses a sign. He has become hypervigilant about Arjun's health in ways that have begun to strain their relationship. He texts his son several times a day. He monitors Arjun's energy levels the way he once monitored vital signs on a hospital monitor. Arjun, who wants to be a normal eighteen-year-old, has started leaving his phone on silent.

Rajan feels the distance opening between them and does not know how to close it. He and Priya rarely speak about those eighteen months. She has moved forward in a way that both comforts and bewilders him. He wonders sometimes if something broke in him during those ICU nights that simply did not break in her, or whether she is carrying it differently, somewhere he cannot see.

He describes himself as a man who used to love his work. Animation, he explains, is about creating the illusion of life — making still things move. He says this without irony, but the parallel is not lost on him. He spends his days animating vitality while feeling, in some fundamental way, frozen in a hospital corridor four years ago, watching a set of double doors and waiting to learn whether his son would live.

He is here, he says, because Priya asked him to come. But also, quietly, because he is tired of being somewhere else every time he is in the room.
